findings.location: sections/homily/90-note.tex, 'Length and pace': 'The prose was read through in full for sense, sentence length and ease of speech, silently and not aloud.'
findings.problem: The sentence presents a full read-through of the prose as it now stands. The production audit says otherwise. Derive-homily iteration 0 read the earlier draft through in full. Iteration 1 then changed three passages: Jerome's clause in the second movement, 'Matthew's word, in the old translation' in the first, and Augustine's baptism clause in the fifth. Of these, research/production-review.md (Derive-homily, iteration 1, 'Counts, pace and rehearsal') records only that 'the changed sentences were read through in their paragraphs'. Every sentence has been read at some point, so no reader is materially misled. Still, the note states as a single completed event a check that was never made on the current text.
findings.required_result: Either read the current spoken body through in full, silently, and record that in the production audit, or restate the note's sentence so it matches the record. For example: the prose was read through in full at its first drafting, and the passages revised since then were read again in their paragraphs, silently and not aloud.

summary: Cold review of the homily 'All Things Are Ready' (homily.tex, sections/homily/10-homily.tex, sections/homily/90-note.tex), with the homily sections of research/production-review.md and generation-metadata.tex. All nine packet-sealed hashes matched. I read the spoken body through continuously as a listener would hear it. It makes one exegetical argument: the refusal in Mt 22:5 is neglect of the invitation for lawful goods, and Chrysostom (69.1), Aquinas (Super Matt. c. 22, p. 281) and Gregory (38.5) read it that way. The argument then moves through what is refused (Is 25:6, 8; Jerome on Mt 22:2; Gregory 38.3), the guests from the roads (Gregory 38.6), Paul's freedom in plenty and want (Phil 4:12-14; Chrysostom, Hom. in Phil. 15), the garment of charity (Augustine, Sermo 90.5-6 and 95.7; Gregory 38.9), the Collect, the Prayer over the Offerings, the Prayer after Communion and the first Communion antiphon, and ends with a practicable response that returns to the opening invitation. The argument would not survive replacing the readings, because its question, its turn and its response all rest on Mt 22:5, 22:9, 22:11-12, Phil 4:12 and the Collect. The speech contains no anecdote, clerical claim, composed prayer, stage direction or visible apparatus. The parable's first hearers are named from Mt 21:23, and the identification of the first invited with a people is not preached. I checked every quotation and report against the tracked source at its locus: the Douay-Rheims verse files for Is 25:6, 8, Mt 21:23, 22:2-14 and Phil 4:10-14; the Clementine Vulgate at Mt 22:9; NPNF 1/10 at Hom. 69.1-2; NPNF 1/13 at Hom. in Phil. 15; NPNF 1/6 at Sermon XL.5-6 and XLV.7; NPNF 1/8 at Ps 34 (Latin 33), section 14; and the Wikisource Latin of Gregory, Hom. 38.3, 5, 6, 9 and 11. I also checked the retained facsimiles, matched to their SHA-256, by rendering them myself: Jerome on PL 26 col. 159 (Rex iste ... Deus omnipotens est. Facit autem nuptias Domino nostro Iesu Christo et Ecclesiae) and Aquinas on Venice p. 281 (Videbantur habere iustam causam exterius; sed Dominus non recipit: quia nulla temporalia debent detinere de veniendo ad Deum). Every quotation is exact or an unbroken part of its source, and every reported sentence is faithful to it. The descriptions of the orations follow the study's own descriptions of the Latin and do not reproduce the approved English. Every exact locus in the note and every References entry is correct. The standing findings are cleared: HOM-001, the patristic unanimity claim, is replaced by Jerome's own clause, and the advisories HOM-002, HOM-003 and HOM-004 are cleared as their required results ask. I recounted the spoken words at 1,465, which matches the note and the audit: about 11.3 minutes at 130 words a minute and 12.2 at 120, inside the 10-12-minute scope. Sentences average about 14 words, and the longest are colon-led lists or quotations that a speaker can manage. I rebuilt homily.tex from the current sources in my scratch directory. It settled with no box or LaTeX warnings and produced bytes identical to the author's proof (SHA-256 2e0675cc7a45aed64497ec62eebc7647fa4946a26b0ef0e67a543d67f675a7ae, 4 pages), and the speech ends on page 2. The generation record carries this run's provenance header and an accurate account of iteration 1. Limits: no spoken or timed delivery was possible, and none is claimed. I did not compare the NPNF English with the Greek or Latin originals. Visual acceptance belongs to a later stage. I judge it a legitimate choice, open to the preacher under either form of the Gospel, that the speech leaves the king's verdict on the guest and Mt 22:14 to the studies. One advisory is recorded: the note's statement about the read-through does not distinguish the full silent reading of iteration 0 from iteration 1's reading of the changed sentences. Verdict: PASS.
